analysis.one_liner: Limits bank overdraft fees and stops banks from charging them without a customer's consent.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to cap overdraft fees, with 67 House cosponsors, sat in the Financial Services Committee until the Congress ended without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the rules banks must follow when they cover a purchase that overdraws a checking account and then charge a fee for it, often $30 or more per transaction. It would cap those fees at one per month and six per year, require fees to be proportional to the bank's actual cost, and bar banks from charging overdraft or declined-transaction fees on ATM and debit card purchases at all unless the customer first agreed to overdraft coverage in writing. It would also stop banks from quietly reordering transactions to trigger the most fees, and from letting customers overdraw at an ATM without warning. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, especially low- and moderate-income households, who are the ones most likely to overdraw a checking account and get hit with repeated flat fees on small purchases. Anyone who swipes a debit card not knowing the bank will enroll them in paid overdraft coverage benefits from the consent requirement, the monthly and yearly fee caps, and the ban on fees for ATM and debit transactions the bank simply declines to pay.

how_it_helps.text: Caps overdraft fees at no more than one per calendar month and six per calendar year per account, instead of the unlimited repeated fees banks were charging, sometimes several in a single day.

Lets a bank charge an overdraft fee only if the customer first consented in writing or electronically, ending automatic enrollment in paid overdraft programs that many consumers did not know they had.
Requires overdraft fees to be reasonable and proportional to the bank's actual cost of processing the transaction, rather than a flat fee charged the same for a $4 coffee as for a large check.

Bans the bank from charging a fee when the overdraft happens only because the bank placed a hold larger than the actual purchase, and requires transactions to be posted in an order that avoids avoidable fees.
Prohibits any fee for declining an ATM withdrawal or debit card transaction, and requires a warning and a chance to cancel at ATMs and branch tellers before a transaction triggers fees.
Blocks banks from reporting a customer's overdraft use to credit bureaus when the overdraft and fees are paid off under the program, and bars unfair or deceptive marketing of overdraft coverage.

analysis.who_pays: Banks and other depository institutions, which collected large, largely automatic fee revenue from overdraft programs, would lose that revenue. Banks warned the loss would push costs onto other services, such as eliminating free checking.

drawbacks.text: Banks keep the discretion to simply reject an overdraft once the fee caps are reached, so a check or payment a customer expected to be covered could instead bounce, with its own consequences.

Banks argue overdraft coverage is a convenience that saves customers from declined cards and bounced checks, and that fee limits would push them to decline transactions or recover the lost revenue by raising other account fees or dropping free checking; the bill's one-year freeze on fee increases was designed partly to prevent banks from raising fees ahead of the rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most consumers the protections outweigh the costs: the bill targets fees charged automatically on small purchases without the customer's knowledge, a practice its own findings describe as burdening low- and moderate-income households. The real trade-off is on the bank side: fee revenue would shrink, and consumers who actually rely on having purchases covered past the caps could see transactions declined or other account fees rise. The bill could have been designed more sharply for heavy overdraft users, but its core consent and fee-cap rules are straightforward consumer protections.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress expired, so it never came up for a vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn Maloney introduced the Overdraft Protection Act of 2009 on October 22, 2009, with 15 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.
The bill's stated findings were that flat overdraft fees charged repeatedly, sometimes several in one day, placed significant financial burdens on low- and moderate-income consumers.

The bill attracted 66 cosponsors in addition to its sponsor, 65 of the chamber's 253 Democrats and 1 of its 178 Republicans, but the House Financial Services Committee never scheduled it for consideration.

The complete action history shows only two actions: introduction and referral to committee. No markup, no report, no floor vote, and no Senate action ever followed before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

Because the bill died, overdraft fee rules were left to be set through regulation rather than statute; the Federal Reserve and, later, the new consumer bureau took up overdraft rulemaking on their own instead of Congress legislating the caps directly.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and other depository institutions are better off, because the fee limits, consent requirement, and ATM fee ban never took effect and overdraft fee revenue was untouched by law. Consumers who pay overdraft fees lost the protections the bill would have given them.

for.name: Carolyn Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 15 original cosponsors; the bill was referred to committee the day she introduced it.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Barney Frank (D-MA), who was himself an original cosponsor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never scheduled it for markup, a hearing, or a floor recommendation during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic: 65 of the bill's 66 additional cosponsors were House Democrats, with a single Republican joining.

industries.note: Overdraft fees are a major, largely automatic fee-revenue stream: a flat fee of $30 or more charged each time a customer overdraws, often several times in a day on small debit purchases. The bill would cap the fees, require customer consent before charging them, and ban them entirely on ATM and debit transactions the bank declines to pay, eliminating most of that revenue. Banks' interest in keeping the fee income ran against the consumers the bill was written to protect.
